title: What changed
dek: Most family archives publish only what they found. This one publishes what it looked for, what it found, what it did not find, and what it had to take back.
lead: This page is the archive's working record. Each entry is one research pass: the sources opened, what came out of them, and which pages of this site changed as a result. Where a pass produced an error that was later corrected, it says so and links to the correction rather than quietly editing the history.

days.title: Hannah was a Berkeley woman all along
did: Opened a subscription site for the first time in this archive's life.
Found the 1851 census at Drivers Fields — the same house as 1841 — which states Hannah's birthplace outright: BERKELEY, GLOUCESTERSHIRE.
Found the marriage: Hannah Saniger to James Wakefield, Bristol, 17 October 1831. The first English record of it, and the first English record of any kind to give her the surname.
Learned that James Wakefield was born at STROUD, and that there were two more children — Jabez, born about 1843, and Zillah, about 1846 — neither of whom this archive had ever heard of.
Established that Berkeley's register CAN be searched after 1677, with parents named. The five untestable Saniger generations were behind a paywall, not behind a gap.
Marked /chew-magna and /bristol-chapels as wrong at the top, and left them up.
Filed the two largest errors this archive has made: an edifice on a single 1841 tick, and the habit of turning “not reachable from here” into “not there”.
Added a warning to the top of /coverage saying what every null on it is really measuring.
Found the marriage of Robert D'Arcy and Jean Ward — Portsea St Mary, 21 June 1779 — which this archive has carried on a family tree since it began.

Established by control test that FindMyPast covers Portsea St Mary continuously from 1770 to 1792, so Joseph D'Arcy having no brothers or sisters baptised there is now a real result instead of an artefact.

Tested every Saniger generation the archive had called untestable. Thomas baptised 1744 father Thomas; Thomas married CATHERINE COTTON at Berkeley in April 1769; John baptised five weeks later; Thomas buried 1819 aged 75; John buried 1825 aged 55.
Found John Saniger's other children at Berkeley — 1801, 1803, 1808 — with the tree putting Hannah's birth in July 1805 exactly between them.
Corrected the tree's death date for John Saniger by ten months.
Built /behind-the-paywall.

Found Samuel Sneyd alive in the 1851 census — Well Street, Hanley, GROCER, born Madeley — with his wife Elizabeth beside him, born OSWESTRY, SHROPSHIRE. That settles the unreadable “Staly Cladwin” of 1861.
Found Elizabeth Oliver's baptism at Oswestry St Oswald's, 19 May 1782, father David, mother Mary — two digits from the tree's date, and a generation the archive did not have.
Tested the tree's Audlem marriage against a parish indexed twice over. Twenty Smiths marry there in the same decade and no Sneyd does, in any spelling, ever.
Found James Wakefield's baptism at Stroud, 6 April 1806, father Richard, mother ELIZABETH WEBB — which explains the Matilda Webb who has been sitting unexplained in his 1841 household.
Marked /berkeley, /sanigers and /portsea where the subscription has overtaken them.
Re-ran the audit: British 145, Australian 96 — 60% to 40%, from 42% at the start.

Found Ellen Wakefield's baptism (Bristol, 26 October 1834, father James, mother Hannah) and her burial (St Paul, Portland Square, 12 July 1840, AGED FIVE). She was never left behind in 1854; she died fourteen years before the ship.

Established by control test why Hannah's own baptism still cannot be found: only the partial FamilySearch index reaches Berkeley, and FindMyPast's Gloucestershire Baptisms does not cover the parish at all.
Searched for John Saniger's marriage at Berkeley and found none, so Lydia remains unnamed by any record.
Put the original Berkeley register and Robert D'Arcy's 1827 death notice at the top of the errand list.
Drove the newspaper archive's date filters by hand and found Robert D'Arcy's death notices — seventeen of them, in England, Ireland and Scotland.
Confirmed his death as 13 May 1827 from papers printed within four days of it, replacing a Victorian printed roll as the authority.
Found his funeral, which nobody here knew about: interred at Chatham WITH MILITARY HONOURS on Saturday 19 May 1827 — the exact date of entry 1571 in the parish register.
And established that the press names nobody he was related to. Not one of the seventeen gives even his forename. The best remaining route to his parentage is now closed.
Pushed the Saniger line back two more generations: Thomas baptised Berkeley 12 December 1711, father William; William baptised there 12 October 1679, father William. Both match the tree to the day.
Found Thomas Saniger's marriage to Catherine Cotton — and then failed to find Catherine anywhere else, which is the one new question this opened.
Traced Jabez and Zillah Wakefield to Queensland, where they married in 1863 and 1871.
Corrected my own claim that Jabez and Zillah were children nobody here had heard of. They are on the passenger register this archive published in July.
Built /saniger-line and /wakefields, and added the Berkeley baptism gap and the newspaper archive to /coverage.

Rebuilt Robert D'Arcy's career from the commission registers and the officer promotions: first commissioned in 1778 as a PRACTITIONER ENGINEER, then Major 1802, Lieutenant-Colonel 1805, Brevet Colonel and Colonel in 1813 — every step citable to the London Gazette by issue and page.
Found that Joseph D'Arcy went into the ROYAL ARTILLERY, listed from 1795 to 1844.
Discarded a Robert D'Arcy gazetted Cornet of the 17th Light Dragoons in 1804 — the ranks make him a different man — and recorded the exclusion.
Built /the-corps.
Found Jean Ward's baptism at SOUTH LEITH — 19 July 1754, father JOSEPH WARD, mother MARTHA GARDEN — in the parish this archive had repeatedly called untranscribed.
Noticed that her father's name was Joseph, and that Joseph is what she and Robert called their son at Portsea in 1780.
Found George Pitt D'Arcy in the Peninsular War officers' roll for 1808, 39th Foot — the regiment he was still with in 1826.
Filed the South Leith claim as an error, and built /jean-ward.
days.found: The answer was the one the family tree gave before any of this started; the family's oldest English records were behind a subscription rather than lost; and a general who was national news for a fortnight was buried without a single newspaper naming his father.

days.title: 91 Well Street, and what the indexes actually hold
did: Found Samuel Sneyd's burial: Hanley St John the Evangelist, 23 September 1855, aged 77, of 91 WELL ST. The tree said 20 September 1856 at No 3.

Tested the year against the death index. Every Samuel Sneyd death registered in England and Wales between 1854 and 1858 — there is exactly one, September quarter 1855 at Stoke. The tree is a year out.
Confirmed his widow's death in the same index: Elizabeth Sneyd, December quarter 1861, Stoke, which is the tree's 1 December 1861 to the quarter.
Noted that the burial age of 77 puts his birth about 1778 — independent support for the Madeley baptism of 1781 this archive corrected to a day earlier, and ten years off the tree's 1769.
Read Collinson's Somerset on Chew Magna: six miles from Bristol, 830 inhabitants, and “in former days … a LARGE CLOTHING TOWN” — the trade that runs through every Saniger found so far.
Corrected two numbers I had invented on /chew-magna that same morning.
Identified Chew Magna as a PECULIAR with its own probate jurisdiction, which changes where a Saniger will would be found.

Control-tested Cheshire and Shropshire: the Audlem marriage and the Oswestry baptism the tree names cannot be tested, because neither place is transcribed. Cheshire returns two John Smiths in twenty years.
Built /coverage — ten index holdings, measured rather than assumed.
Register now 210 records.

Found Elizabeth Sanigar at Battles Lane, Chew Magna, in the 1841 census — in a spade-maker's house, which is the trade Collinson said the parish still had. The Bristol clerk of 1851 was not mishearing the name of a parish.
Checked whether the twelve Bristol chapel registers can actually be read online. All twelve are digitised:false at Kew. Filed as an error, because this archive said the opposite the same morning.
Looked for a route to Portsea's register beyond FreeREG's two years and found none through Discovery.
Re-ran the 1851 search for the Wakefields. Still nothing, and still an absence from a partial transcript rather than a finding.
days.found: Six of the ten index holdings measured are parishes the family tree names, and six of them are partial, empty or unreachable. An archive built on free indexes will systematically fail to test its own tree, and will mistake that failure for a finding unless it measures every time.

days.title: Swanhanger, Well Street, and two years of Portsea
did: Searched the whole TNA catalogue for Saniger rather than one collection: 71 records, including the Berkeley estate deeds that follow Edward Saniger from clothier in 1692 to gentleman in 1709.

Proved that Saniger is a worn-down SWANHANGER. One deed of 1377 is catalogued by Berkeley Castle under the man, de Swonhongre, and by Birmingham Archives under the place, Swanhanger — and Gloucestershire Archives glosses a third document “Swanhanger … [Saniger in Hinton]”.

Searched probate for the first time. Two wills — Elizabeth Saniger, widow of Thornbury, 1833, and Samuel Sanigear of Chipping Sodbury, 1832 — and a defamation suit brought by Christian Saniger in 1768.
Re-read Bigland properly: six more Saniger entries in volume one, six neighbouring households styled “of Saniger” who are not called Saniger, and none at all in volume two.
Catalogued every Bristol chapel register in RG 4. There are 36, not the 5 this archive's errand list assumed, and exactly 12 can hold a birth between 1805 and 1815.
Found Samuel Sneyd's household. The 1861 census at Well St, Hanley — a grocer's shop — holds his widow Elizabeth, aged 82, born Shropshire, eight months before she died.
Established by control test that FreeCEN holds only 1861 for Staffordshire, so the 1841 and 1851 searches everyone assumed had failed were never possible.
Tested how much of Portsea's register stands behind Joseph D'Arcy's 1780 baptism. Twenty-two months of it.
Found Robert D'Arcy in the London Gazette of 19 July 1813, gazetted Colonel of the Royal Engineers.
Rewrote /berkeley's conclusion, built /portsea and /bristol-chapels, and filed two more errors.
Re-ran the nationality audit. British evidence now outnumbers Australian for the first time: 107 to 96.

Searched the 1851 census for Sanigers around Bristol and found a household at Oxford Road, St Philip and Jacob — the parish next to the Wakefields' — whose head and whose widowed mother were both born at CHEW MAGNA, SOMERSET.
Control-tested Chew Magna in FreeREG: two Smith entries in twenty-one years against a hundred at Walcot. The transcript is a fragment, so the parish cannot be searched from here.
Built /chew-magna and put the register at the top of the errand list.

Control-tested the city of Bristol in FreeREG: 289 Smith entries from 75 Gloucestershire parishes, 1800–1820, and exactly one from inside Bristol. The city is not in the index, which is why every Bristol search here has come back empty.
days.found: The family's name is a hillside above the Severn where the swans were; the archive's oldest English record survives inside a two-year window nobody had measured; and Hannah Saniger's birthplace has, for the first time, a county and a parish worth the fare to Taunton.

days.title: Saniger from 1272, and Bigland fills the gap
did: Searched the Berkeley Castle Muniments: nine deeds name people OF SANIGER between about 1272 and 1473, and not one of them is called Saniger.
Found Bigland's 1791 Collections on archive.org and read the Berkeley section: “Saniger, long held by an old Family of the same Name”, with the monumental inscriptions.
Recovered from those monuments a century of Berkeley material the parish transcript does not hold — Saniger inscriptions from 1692 to 1750 with ages and relationships.
Identified the Hinton manor court rolls, GCR/231 and 258, as the record type that would catch the family where the register cannot.
Rewrote /berkeley's conclusion, which said the archive should stop calling this a Berkeley family. It was wrong.
Searched the same catalogue for Wakefield of Bristol, Sneyd of Madeley and D'Arcy wills in Kent. Nothing usable in any of the three.
days.found: The place is two hundred years older than the surname, and it is documented from before 1291. An antiquary copied the family's gravestones in 1791 and they have been sitting in a scanned book ever since.

days.title: Saniger is a place — and the audit starts to move
did: Found the 1851 census household of Thomas Sinegar, labourer, at 7 Oxford Road, Bristol — born, with his wife Martha, at BERKLEY, Gloucestershire.
Established that Sanigers were still at Berkeley itself in 1841, in a parish whose transcript stops in 1677.
Found in TNA's catalogue that SANIGER IS A PLACE in Berkeley parish, with the family holding land there from 1601.
Found the will of John Maddock Jones of Ruabon, who married Robert D'Arcy's daughter — a Welsh branch the archive has never had.
Found Robert D'Arcy in the printed Army List of 1778, and Francis D'Arcy separately in the same volume.
Was blocked by Cloudflare at Welsh Newspapers Online and irishgenealogy.ie — four free British and Irish databases shut in one day.
Re-ran the nationality audit: the Australian share has fallen from 57% to 53%.
days.found: The surname is toponymic. Saniger is a hamlet in Berkeley parish, a John Saniger holds land there as a yeoman in 1601, and an Edward Saniger of Saniger is a clothier in 1692 and a gentleman by 1709.

days.title: Back to Britain — and an audit that says the archive had drifted
did: Audited the register by nationality of source: 95 Australian records against 70 British. The archive had drifted to the wrong side of the world and nobody had measured it.
Named the five TNA RG 4 registers that would hold Hannah's baptism, replacing a vague instruction to write to Bristol.
Found a Sinegar brewer's household at St Philip and St Jacob with a daughter Lydia — candidate kin, labelled as such.
Established that William the weaver's baptism is in no transcribed Staffordshire register at all, and that Madeley has no Bishop's Transcripts in FreeREG.
Searched Denbighshire for John Maddock Jones of Ruabon. Well covered, and he is not in it.
Read the Gazette for Joseph, Constantine and George Pitt D'Arcy. Nothing, with an OCR caveat.
Was blocked by Cloudflare at irishgenealogy.ie — three Irish lines, one free database, and no way in from here.
days.found: 57% of this archive's records now come from Australian sources. The brief was always the British ancestry.

days.title: The Gazette, the Birches, and a jurisdiction still shut
did: Found ten London Gazette notices naming Robert D'Arcy between 1793 and 1819, and read one in full.
Identified the Birch household: Margaret and Elizabeth Ann were daughters of John Birch and Annie Reeves.
Traced nine Wakefield grandchildren through the Queensland index.
Tried the NSW BDM index and was stopped by a bot check — recorded as an errand rather than a null.
Corrected a stale blocked entry: Museums of History NSW is live and the State Archives catalogue is reachable.
days.found: Robert D'Arcy's promotions are in the government's own gazette, issue and page, where this archive has been citing a printed roll compiled from them.

days.title: The Sneyd chain closes, and four other lines tested
did: Reconstituted all 551 Staffordshire Sneyd records into 94 households.
Found William Sneyd the weaver's family at Madeley — thirteen children, 1769 to 1794.
Corrected the tree: their Samuel is baptised 1781, not 1769.
Ran the Queensland immigration index for every other family in the archive. Only the Wakefields came assisted.
Exhausted Bristol's four transcribed registers. Neither family is in them.
Searched Gloucestershire for Richard Wakefield and found one weak candidate.
Searched Queensland for the three eldest Wakefield daughters. They did not sail and never followed.
Tested the Somerset-side-of-Bristol hypothesis: Bedminster and Long Ashton are covered and empty; Temple, Redcliffe and Brislington are not transcribed.
Searched Hampshire and Kent for the other eight D'Arcy children. Two of ten are in the registers.
days.found: Three of the four Sneyd links are now documented, and the missing one is a baptism of 1746. The line runs weaver, servant, gaol governor.

days.title: Chatham — the parish the Corps lived in
did: Searched Chatham St Mary the Virgin, where Robert D'Arcy served and died, and which nobody had ever tried.
Found seven D'Arcy records including three burials the archive has only ever known second-hand.
Read Robert's burial: age 76 — the primary source behind the tree's “1751”, seen for the first time.
Found Jean Ward's burial, at sixty-six, and Constantine's, entered with his rank.
Found George Pitt D'Arcy in a parish register as “Bt: Major 39th Foot”, christening a daughter eight days before the England sailed.
Searched six more counties around Bristol for Hannah Saniger, with controls. Nothing.
days.found: Chatham holds the D'Arcy family's whole English ending: a general, his wife, his brother officer, his daughter's marriage and his son's rank — none of it ever looked at.

days.title: The ship: General Hewitt, Brisbane, 16 December 1854
did: Found Queensland's assisted-immigration index published as open data after ArchivesSearch itself refused to run a search.
Found the whole family on one voyage and downloaded the register scan, DR38490.
Read the register: James a mason, Hiram a plumber, and Miriam — entered as Marion — shipped at fourteen as a domestic servant.
Established that the register does NOT give Hannah's own county: hers is a ditto of her husband's.
Searched Hanley — the parish the tree names and nobody had tried — and found Samuel Charles Sneyd's baptism with both parents.
Followed up the Madeley marriage of William Sneyd and Mary Blackbourne, which had been in the results all day.
Corrected this morning's overstatement that the Sneyd line was unevidenced. Two of its four links are documented.
days.found: The emigration, dated to the day and named. The archive knew the family reached Queensland; it did not know how, when, or on what.

days.title: The county reconstituted, and the Bristol migration
did: Opened all 556 Gloucestershire Saniger records individually instead of searching them by name.
Assembled 81 households from the 196 baptisms that name a father, splitting same-named couples wherever 25 years separate consecutive baptisms.
Asked all 81 whether any could be Hannah's. None can.
Published /sanigers: the households, the trades, seventeen spellings rather than eleven, and the 29 Sanigers in Bristol on census night 1841.
days.found: The Gloucestershire Sanigers are a Stroudwater cloth-trade family — weavers, tuckers, curriers — at Cam and Dursley, not Berkeley. And Hannah is in none of their households, because she was not born in the county.

days.title: The maiden name, settled five times over
did: Searched the Queensland death index by MOTHER's name rather than by the deceased — the search this archive should have run a week ago.
Found five of Hannah's children's death registrations, each naming her, across 41 years and four spellings.
Found Hannah's own registration, naming her father John Saniger — entered by the clerk as “John Jenniger”.
Found James Wakefield's registration, naming HIS father Richard Wakefield: a new generation.
Found Miriam's marriage to William Hartley Sneyd, 15 November 1859, and corrected her age from twenty-one to nineteen.
Added 14 records and 9 recorded relationships to the register.
Asked Madeley for the two Sneyd baptisms the tree actually names — 1746 and 1769 — and found neither, in a parish transcribed continuously with 110 Sneyd records.
Searched FreeBMD for Lyddya Sinegar's death in England and found nothing under any spelling.
Recorded that the 1861 and 1871 censuses cannot help: the family had emigrated by 1857.
days.found: The archive spent a week trying to prove “Saniger” from the English end. It was written down five times in Queensland by five different clerks, and nobody had thought to search the index by the mother's name.

days.title: Portsea, Madeley, and three counties that hold nothing
did: Found Joseph D'Arcy baptised at Portsea St Mary on 19 March 1780, father Robert, mother Jean — the first record of Robert D'Arcy in an English parish register this archive has ever had.
Read the Madeley baptism that killed the Keele graft, and then found a William son of William Sneyd buried there in September 1744.

Established that FreeREG holds nothing for County Limerick, nothing for South Leith and nothing for St Quivox — three of this archive's oldest dead ends are dead ends in the database, not in the record.
Tested and rejected the Berkley-in-Somerset hypothesis for Hannah Saniger.
days.found: Robert D'Arcy and Jean Ward, named together as the parents of a child baptised at Portsea in 1780. His parentage is still unknown; his marriage is no longer a claim.

days.title: The Saniger chain, tested at last — and it breaks
did: Checked FreeREG's coverage for Bristol BEFORE searching it. Four registers, 1,551 records, and St Paul is not among them — so the Wakefield join was never testable there and any null would have been a lie.
Found that Dursley St James (1577–1951) and Cam St George (1568–1939) cover the whole Saniger chain, which /berkeley had implied was untestable.
Searched the county: 494 Saniger records 1670–1830, and three baptisms matching the tree's dates almost exactly, all at Dursley.
Opened all three. The fathers are Abraham, John and Samuel — three unrelated men. The chain is a coincidence of dates.
Established that no Saniger baptism exists in Gloucestershire 1801–1809, in a window that is well covered.
Established that in 139 Gloucestershire records spanning 1790–1900, no Saniger ever marries a Wakefield.
Found Miriam Wakefield's birth registration in FreeBMD: June quarter 1840, Bristol, volume 11, page 183 — the only one in England in five years.
Control-tested the FreeBMD harness (21,248 Wakefield marriages, 1838–1842) before reporting any absence from it.
Rewrote /berkeley around the result and added the GRO certificate to /errands as the cheapest decisive document on the site.

Then found the household in the 1841 census and published /drivers-fields — James and Hannah Wakefield at St Paul, Bristol, with Miriam aged one, and a seventy-year-old Sinegar widow living with them.
days.found: Three Dursley baptisms match the tree's dates for the middle of the Saniger line. Opening them shows three different fathers. The oldest claim in this archive is weaker than it was this morning — and for the first time there is a £2.50 document that would settle it. And then the census produced the couple themselves, at the street the tree had remembered and the county it had got wrong.

days.title: The DNA, and the branding brought into line
did: Published /dna — one living descendant's autosomal estimate against the tree's own prediction, computed twice, once with both grafts cut.
Corrected an error in that analysis within the hour: the first version put the predicted Scottish share at 0.02% and announced the DNA was contradicting the tree. It was not. Recorded as error nine.
Brought the homepage onto the .hero banner every sibling archive uses. The rules had been in this site's stylesheet, unused, since it was built.
Built /search over the whole archive, with the eleven spellings of Saniger folded together.
Added /searched, /changes and /errands — publishing work that had been sitting in notes/ and requests/ on disk.
days.found: That cutting both grafts — 98 people, thirteen generations, four royal houses — moves the predicted ancestry by 0.39 of a percentage point.

days.title: Berkeley, and the audit that moved the floor
did: Searched the Gloucestershire parish registers instead of another family's website.
Published /berkeley: 44 Sainger entries, three Williams, one good candidate and a father the archive never had.
Caught a false story before publishing it as fact, and left it on the page as a worked example.
Audited every 'defended' ancestor and published the result even though it was bad.
days.found: Of 144 ancestors the archive called documented, eight rest on a record set. Above generation seven, exactly one of sixty does. The honest figure is about seven generations, not twelve.

days.title: The worst error, and the register
did: Told the family their own founding brief was wrong. It was not; I had read the root person's spouse instead of her parents. It stood on the site for a day.
Published /register — every named individual the archive has met anywhere, with the source beside each one.
Put a pedigree chart on all 473 person pages, with the border encoding how each relationship is known.
days.found: Of 473 pedigree charts, 19 contain a single edge written in a record.

days.title: The inquest nobody knew about
did: Read QSA coronial file DR103140 in full and published it plainly at /inquest-1902.
Published /finding-arthur from the Red Cross file.
Rewrote /great-war around four men instead of one.
days.found: A suicide in Victoria Park in 1902 — and, in the widow's sworn deposition, the name of his father, closing a generation four research passes had been circling.

close: If you find something this page does not record, that is a gap in the record-keeping and worth telling me about.
